founder: Hillel Coren (CPO, developer) with Shalom Stark (CEO) and David Bomba (CTO, joined 2015)
founderSource: invoiceninja.com/our-story (founders page) + github.com/hillelcoren/invoice-ninja + CardRates Dec 2023 interview with Stark
teamSize: 3 core (Stark CEO, Coren CPO, Bomba CTO) per 2023 interview; plus open-source contributors
targetCustomer: Freelancers and small businesses needing invoicing, payments and expense tracking.
customerSegment: B2B SMB: freelancers and small service businesses worldwide.
coreProblem: Freelancers and SMBs need professional invoicing and payments without enterprise cost or lock-in.
problemFrequency: Weekly: every invoice cycle and payment chase.
problemSeverity: HIGH: late or unprofessional billing directly delays income for cash-strapped freelancers.
existingAlternatives: Word/Excel invoices, FreshBooks, Wave, QuickBooks, pen-and-paper billing.
currentUserWorkflow: Freelancer tracks hours in spreadsheets, builds invoices in Word/Excel, chases payment by email with no tracking.
productSolution: Source-available invoicing suite with hosted SaaS option: invoice, get paid online, track time/expenses in one place.
coreFeature: Recurring/open-source invoicing with online payments, time tracking, expenses and client portal.
initialMVP: First iteration built in a few weeks after late-2013 coffee meeting; live serving freelancers by March 2014.
featuresNotInMVP: Payment gateway breadth, recurring billing depth, time tracking, expenses, client portal polish; marketing spend stayed $0 for years.
currentFeatureSet: Invoices, quotes, recurring billing, 40+ payment gateways, time tracking, expenses, projects, client portal, reports; hosted SaaS plus self-hosted.
pricingModel: Freemium subscription: free tier, paid Pro/Enterprise hosted plans, plus $40/yr white-label license for self-hosters.
pricingTiers: Free; Pro and Enterprise hosted tiers (exact current prices NOT verified, check site); $40/yr white-label self-host license.
freeTier: Free hosted tier exists; self-hosted code free (white-label removal $40/yr license per GitHub readme).
trial: Demo available; free tier; trial mechanics NOT verified.
revenueEvidence: $550K ARR as of Sept 2025 per GetLatka (SECONDARY ESTIMATE, not founder-disclosed); founder-disclosed only: $10K MRR in 3 years; REVENUE NOT PUBLICLY DISCLOSED by founders.
mrrEvidence: $10K MRR reached in 3 years (Startup Founder Stories); $550K ARR Sept 2025 is GetLatka ESTIMATE, not founder-disclosed.
arrEvidence: $550K ARR Sept 2025 per GetLatka (SECONDARY ESTIMATE); founder-disclosed ARR NOT published.
customerEvidence: 200,000+ accounts created; 85% of customers on hosted SaaS; three-person team handles all support personally with Slack/Discord/GitHub community help.
growthEvidence: $10K MRR within 3 years; $550K ARR by Sept 2025 (GetLatka); user base grew via $0 marketing spend.
timeToLaunch: Weeks from coffee (late 2013) to live product (March 2014).
validationMethod: Live product with real freelancers invoicing within weeks; HN front-page feedback validated demand before any monetization push.
firstUserAcquisition: Hacker News front page launch in March 2014 with founder answering feedback live in comments.
first100Users: HN front-page launch plus open-source discovery; 200,000 accounts milestone reached within a few years per company timeline.
mainDistribution: Open-source discovery (GitHub/self-host) plus SEO, with word of mouth from freelance communities.
secondaryDistribution: Slack/Discord/GitHub community where users help users; timeline notes 200,000 accounts milestone.
seoStrategy: Ranks for invoicing keywords; open-source angle earns developer backlinks; docs and template content support long-tail.
xStrategy: No documented X/Twitter growth engine; founder blogs and release notes carry updates.
redditStrategy: No documented Reddit program; organic mentions in freelance subreddits Secondary at best.
indieHackersStrategy: No documented Indie Hackers launch; community presence via open-source channels instead.
productHuntStrategy: No notable Product Hunt launch documented.
hackerNewsStrategy: Launch-day front-page thread March 2014 drove first wave; founder engagement converted readers to users.
directOutreach: Founder personally answered Hacker News launch thread comments (March 2014).
partnerships: Payment gateway integrations (40+) act as distribution partnerships; no major co-marketing deals disclosed.
referralViral: Weak direct loop; growth via open-source sharing and freelancer word of mouth rather than in-product virality.
techStack: Laravel/PHP backend (per GitHub); hosted + self-hosted; frontend/mobile details NOT PUBLIC.
infrastructure: Hosted SaaS plus self-hosted PHP installs; exact cloud provider NOT PUBLIC.
aiUsage: No AI usage documented; pre-AI-era product (2014) with traditional codebase.
devMethod: Nights-and-weekends style sprint by developer co-founder; community feedback loop via GitHub issues and forum threads.
soloFeasibility: Feasible: two founders plus one CTO run it; solo harder due to payments/support surface but proven by years of 3-person ops.
technicalComplexity: MEDIUM: payments, tax rules and multi-tenant SaaS plus self-host install matrix.
productComplexity: MEDIUM: invoicing core is simple; payments, taxes and multi-currency add long-tail scope.
infraComplexity: MEDIUM: must run reliable hosted SaaS plus support self-hosted installs across environments.
operationalComplexity: MEDIUM: payments/tax edge cases and self-host support questions, but small team sustains it.
supportBurden: MEDIUM: billing/payment questions are urgent, offset by community self-support on Slack/Discord/GitHub.
salesComplexity: LOW: self-serve signup, demo available, no sales team; three founders do support directly.
differentiation: Only serious open-source invoicing suite: self-host free forever, pay only for hosted convenience or white-label removal.
competitiveMoat: Open-source distribution (GitHub discovery, self-hosters converting to hosted) plus 10+ year brand and hecho ecosistema of integrations; hard to displace on price.
competitors: Wave, FreshBooks, Xero, QuickBooks, Zoho Invoice.
competitiveWeaknesses: Design polish lags VC-funded rivals; tiny team limits support bandwidth and feature velocity; license is source-available with paid white-label, not pure OSI open source.
retention: Strong: billing data lock-in plus annual white-label renewals; exact churn NOT PUBLIC.
legalPrivacy: Handles financial/tax data across jurisdictions; self-host option sidesteps many data-residency objections. Details NOT PUBLIC.
acquisitionDifficulty: LOW: open source plus SEO compounded with $0 spend to 200,000 accounts.
monetizationDifficulty: LOW: clear paid triggers (hosting convenience, white-label, gateways); free riders self-host at near-zero cost to company.
zeroUpfront: YES: code-built product, free GitHub distribution, $0 marketing; runnable today with Laravel + cheap hosting.
mrr100: HIGH: recurring pain, proven $10 price points, free tier funnels to paid; zero-CAC channels demonstrated.
learn: Open-sourcing the product IS the marketing: developers self-host, then convert to paid hosted; answer every early comment yourself.
notCopy: Do not clone feature breadth on day one; the wedge was simple invoices plus payments, everything else came over a decade.
primaryEvidence: Our-story: 'Bootstrapped, founder-run... 100% bootstrapped (self-funded, no VC overlords!)'; Stark (CardRates 2023): built first iteration 'in a few weeks'; GitHub: Laravel codebase, white-label $40/yr. CONSTAT: aggregators call v5 'source-available' rather than OSI open source.

founder: Nathan Powell (original MVP) and Michael Koper (joined 2014; sole owner since 2019 buyout)

teamSize: Solo (Michael Koper) since early-2019 buyout of Nathan Powell

coreProblem: Creative freelancers and agencies waste hours formatting proposals in InDesign/PDF/email with no tracking or signing.
problemFrequency: Weekly: agencies send multiple proposals per week per rep.

featuresNotInMVP: CRM integrations, payments, versioning history (still 'coming soon' on Business plan), permissions, API/webhooks.

revenueEvidence: REVENUE NOT PUBLICLY DISCLOSED; founder describes 'calm, profitable small business' supporting a frugal family life in Spain; no figures published.
mrrEvidence: $1,000 MRR reached quickly after beta (Koper 10-year post; Starter Story); current MRR NOT PUBLIC.
arrEvidence: REVENUE NOT PUBLICLY DISCLOSED; no ARR figure published by founder.

growthEvidence: $1,000 MRR quickly after beta; then multi-year plateau openly discussed; solo-run since 2019 with slight growth.
timeToLaunch: A few months of evenings/weekends from join to beta; Koper quit Cabify Dec 2014 with 4 months runway.
validationMethod: Prototype in front of potential users for feedback pre-beta; beta fans plus fast $1K MRR validated willingness to pay.
firstUserAcquisition: Prototype shown to potential users for feedback, then beta launch to blog audience and design community contacts.
first100Users: Beta fan group converted quickly to $1,000 MRR; blog (running since 2013) plus content marketing drove first 100 (Powell: 'via the blog, you know, content marketing').
mainDistribution: Content marketing/blog (since 2013, some posts near-viral in niche) plus SEO; founder calls traffic the binding constraint.
secondaryDistribution: Integration marketplaces (HubSpot, Pipedrive) plus one AppSumo lifetime deal (traffic spike, mixed-quality cohort).

directOutreach: Founder jumps on Zoom with customers for setup and feedback (ongoing, per homepage).
partnerships: HubSpot and Pipedrive marketplace listings opened larger-business segment (Starter Story).
referralViral: Weak loop; growth leans on integrations and stories, not in-product virality.
techStack: Ruby on Rails (verified); remainder NOT PUBLIC.
infrastructure: Ruby on Rails app; hosting provider NOT PUBLIC.
aiUsage: Pricing page lists Claude among build-your-own integration options (2026); no native AI features documented.
devMethod: Evenings/weekends rewrite: Nathan redesigned v2 from scratch while Koper rewrote Rails MVP; prototype-first with user feedback.
soloFeasibility: Proven: solo-run profitable since 2019 buyout; support load manageable at this scope.
technicalComplexity: LOW: standard Rails CRUD plus e-signatures and notifications.
productComplexity: LOW-MEDIUM: focused proposal flow; deliberately avoids enterprise CPQ scope.
infraComplexity: LOW: standard Rails SaaS; webhooks/API add modest surface.
operationalComplexity: LOW: intentionally small; founder does support, jumps on Zoom, guards time for serious triallists only.
supportBurden: LOW-MEDIUM: solo founder handles chat/email + Zoom; card-upfront trial screens out casuals.
salesComplexity: LOW: self-serve trial, demo offered on Business plan; founder-led Zoom closes.
differentiation: Calm profitable micro-SaaS with founder-on-Zoom support; deliberately simple vs enterprise proposal suites.
competitiveMoat: 14-year reputation, personal founder support (Zoom onboarding), simplicity positioning against bloated PandaDoc/Proposify.
competitors: Better Proposals, Bidsketch, PandaDoc, Proposify, Qwilr, Word/InDesign.
competitiveWeaknesses: Solo-run: slow feature velocity; plateaued growth acknowledged by founder; AppSumo LTD cohort adds support load with low expansion.
retention: Mixed:Missing-features and wrong-fit churn openly discussed by Powell (2015); exact churn NOT PUBLIC.
legalPrivacy: E-signatures claimed legally binding; GDPR page exists; audit detail NOT PUBLIC.
acquisitionDifficulty: HIGH: founder names traffic the binding constraint; plateau despite 45% trial-to-paid.
monetizationDifficulty: LOW: card-upfront trial filters to payers; 60-day guarantee reduces risk objections.

teamSize: 12 full-time across 6 countries (2020, SaaS Club); current headcount NOT verified

customerSegment: B2B SMB: e-commerce, agencies, coaches, SaaS onboarding and sales teams.
coreProblem: Remote/async sellers cannot build rapport over text email; leads from other time zones go cold before a call.
problemFrequency: Daily: every new lead/signup triggers a welcome moment.
problemSeverity: MEDIUM-HIGH: tripled conversion rates vs text email per founder tests; missed rapport directly loses deals.
existingAlternatives: Text welcome emails, Loom/Vidyard videos, BombBomb, generic email automation.
currentUserWorkflow: Sales teams send templated text welcome emails with low response rates; follow-ups are generic drips.
productSolution: Triggered personal video messages for leads/customers plus a testimonials collector to turn rapport into proof.
coreFeature: One-to-one video messages triggered by funnel events plus testimonial collection (Bonjoro Testimonials, 2022).
initialMVP: Slack-notification hack plus manual phone recordings on Sydney ferry; weekend-built tool that hosted video and emailed it for one Pipedrive/Mailchimp client; charged $15/mo immediately.
featuresNotInMVP: Testimonials product (2022), integrations breadth, team features, automation rules; MVP barely emailed a hosted video.
currentFeatureSet: Video messaging, Testimonials product, integrations (Pipedrive/Mailchimp lineage), automations that 'automate processes, never relationships'; 27 languages claimed.
pricingModel: Tiered subscription across Video Messaging and Testimonials; exact current tiers NOT verified.
pricingTiers: Tiered plans incl. free entry (exact current prices NOT verified, check bonjoro.com/pricing).
freeTier: Free plan exists per secondary reports; exact current tiers NOT verified on site.
trial: Trial exists per secondary reports; mechanics NOT verified.
revenueEvidence: $83.3K/mo (~$1M/yr), profitable, per Starter Story Oct 2024 (SECONDARY ESTIMATE); GetLatka 'grew to $1M over 9 years' snippet consistent; founder-disclosed revenue NOT found.
mrrEvidence: $83.3K/month average per Starter Story Oct 2024 (SECONDARY ESTIMATE); no founder-disclosed MRR found.
arrEvidence: ~$1M/year average per Starter Story Oct 2024 ('makes an average of $1M/year'); founder-disclosed ARR NOT published; treat as SECONDARY ESTIMATE.
customerEvidence: 45,000 users and team of 12 across 6 countries within a few years; early logos Basecamp and ConvertKit; 100,000+ people 'sent a Bonjoro' in first 3 years (about page).
growthEvidence: 0 to 40,000 users in ~3 years 'entirely by word of mouth' (Cubicle to CEO 2021); 45K users per Starter Story 2024.
timeToLaunch: One weekend for MVP; ~10-18 months agency side-project to full-time team shift.
validationMethod: Paywall on ugly beta: paying customers on day one proved demand before any rebuild.
firstUserAcquisition: Agency clients asked to use the internal hack; weekend MVP put on closed beta; $15/mo paywall from day one with paying customers immediately.
first100Users: 100 users within a couple of weeks of beta via client referrals: clients' recipients signed up after receiving videos (built-in viral loop).
mainDistribution: In-product virality: every sent video carries Bonjoro branding and pulls recipients into funnel; seeded by ~50 conversations, half converted.
secondaryDistribution: Word of mouth via early-adopter logos (Basecamp, ConvertKit); founder event circuit pre-COVID; podcasts.
seoStrategy: Secondary; brand-driven and integration content rather than SEO-led growth.
xStrategy: Founder-led storytelling and affiliate recruitment; no scaled X playbook documented.
indieHackersStrategy: No IH launch documented; founder story circulates via podcasts instead.
directOutreach: Founder personally recorded videos for every lead on ferry commute; later onboarding calls with every paid user.
partnerships: Affiliate program paying 30% monthly in perpetuity; unpaid influencer amplification (Pat Flynn and peers).
referralViral: STRONG: core loop — recipients ask 'how was this made' and enter funnel; affiliate 30%-for-life amplifies.
infrastructure: Video hosting and delivery stack; provider details NOT PUBLIC.
devMethod: Weekend MVP hacked with Slack + Zapier + manual video hosting/emailing; iterated on weekends as agency side project.
soloFeasibility: LOW for solo: video infra, two products and high-touch onboarding needed a 12-person team; start narrower.
technicalComplexity: MEDIUM: video capture, hosting, delivery and CRM triggers at scale.
productComplexity: MEDIUM: recording/delivery UX plus CRM triggers; second product doubles surface.
infraComplexity: MEDIUM: video recording/hosting/delivery at scale plus email deliverability.
operationalComplexity: MEDIUM: remote team across 5-6 countries; onboarding calls for every paid user is high-touch by design.
supportBurden: MEDIUM: high-touch onboarding by design; 'sleuth' support team positioning.
salesComplexity: LOW: self-serve plus human onboarding calls; no enterprise sales motion documented.
differentiation: Anti-automation positioning: personal videos at scale with human onboarding for every paid user (cut churn 25%).
competitiveMoat: Viral product loop (every video exposes recipient to Bonjoro) plus onboarding ritual (welcome video to each signup) and affiliate army.
competitiveWeaknesses: Video-tool market crowded (Loom, Vidyard); two-product stretch (messaging + testimonials); small team vs funded rivals.
retention: Onboarding calls with every paid user cut churn 25% (SaaS Club); absolute churn NOT PUBLIC.
legalPrivacy: Video of identifiable people plus testimonials raise consent/retention duties; public policy detail NOT reviewed (UNKNOWN).
acquisitionDifficulty: MEDIUM: viral loop works but video category is noisy; seeding took ~50 conversations.
monetizationDifficulty: LOW-MEDIUM: easy $15 entry, expansion via seats and second product; price pressure from free Loom tier.
zeroUpfront: POSSIBLY: MVP was cheap (weekend + agency engineers), but it was agency-subsidized, not zero-cost; pure solo replication needs video hosting budget.
mrr100: MEDIUM: proven $15+ seats and viral loop, but video infra costs and crowded category raise burn vs solo-friendly tools.
learn: Charge from day one even for ugly MVPs; bake the viral loop into the artifact (every video markets you); onboard every paid user personally to cut churn.
notCopy: Do not copy the later two-product stretch until core loop is saturated; Testimonials split focus per founder's own 'nervous/excited' framing.
primaryEvidence: Barnett (SaaS Origin Stories): 'We spent a weekend with a few beers and pizza, putting a MVP together... We put a paywall down, we got some money'; SaaS Club: 'first day we had it up we had paid customers'; About: 'in just 3 years, over 100,000 of you sent a Bonjoro'. CONTRADICTION: bootstrapped-origin story vs SaaS Club: 'funded by just $1 million AUD from two Australian venture funds' + founder 'We raised money later' — small VC round confirmed, so strictly not pure-bootstrapped.

founder: Becca Berg (CEO, photographer) and Jake Berg (developer, web designer)
founderSource: dubsado.com/blog toddler-mishap origin post (Becca, Feb 2025) + Built In LA Mar 2023 + Boss Project podcast Jul 2020
teamSize: Lean remote team; exact headcount NOT PUBLIC (founders emphasize staying small)
category: all-in-one client management / micro-CRM for creatives
targetCustomer: Creative entrepreneurs: photographers, designers, planners, coaches running client services.
customerSegment: B2B SMB: photographers, creative entrepreneurs, coaches, service freelancers.
coreProblem: Creative service pros juggle 75 logins and paper forms across contracts, invoices and client comms while raising a family and jobs.
problemFrequency: Daily: every booking, contract, invoice and follow-up runs through the gap.
problemSeverity: HIGH: disorganization reads as unprofessional and directly loses bookings in trust-driven creative markets.
existingAlternatives: Paper forms, HoneyBook, 17hats, Bonsai, spreadsheets + PayPal patchworks.
currentUserWorkflow: Paper questionnaires and contracts (one got scribbled on by a toddler), Word invoices, email threads, no unified brand.
productSolution: One brandable hub for proposals, contracts, payments, scheduling and client communication for creative businesses.

featuresNotInMVP: Scheduler depth, automations library, time tracking, templating marketplace; MVP was core forms/contracts/payments flow tested in beta.
currentFeatureSet: Proposals, contracts/e-sign, invoicing/payment plans, scheduler, forms/questionnaires, workflows/automations, client portals, time tracking, reporting.
pricingModel: Single Premier plan subscription, monthly or annual; legacy beta users grandfathered.

freeTier: No free-forever; 'forever' free trial until 3 clients (possible because both founders kept full-time jobs at launch).
trial: Free trial until 3 clients ('forever' until then); no time limit at launch by design.
revenueEvidence: REVENUE NOT PUBLICLY DISCLOSED; scale signal only: 30,000+ customers (2026 podcasts) at ~$400/yr implies material bootstrapped revenue — do NOT present as fact.

arrEvidence: REVENUE NOT PUBLICLY DISCLOSED; no ARR published.
customerEvidence: 30,000+ users/customers claimed across 2025-2026 founder interviews; beloved in photographer/creative communities.
growthEvidence: 300-person list to 30,000+ users over a decade, self-funded; Dubsado 3.0 rebuild in progress (2026 interviews).
timeToLaunch: ~10 months build to beta, plus months of beta hardening before public launch.
validationMethod: 300-person newsletter list before code-complete; beta usage and grandfathered conversions validated willingness to pay.
firstUserAcquisition: Website describing the platform plus newsletter signup shared on social; 300 interested on mailing list before beta (Boss Project 2020).
first100Users: Beta launched to 300-person newsletter list; tested for months to work out kinks before public launch.
mainDistribution: Creative-community word of mouth: photographer Facebook groups, educator affiliates, Becca's personal brand and podcast circuit.
secondaryDistribution: Podcasts and creative-business press; template/workflow sharing acts as viral education.
seoStrategy: Secondary to community; brand + use-case content rather than SEO-led motion.
xStrategy: Minimal; audience lives on Instagram/Facebook/Pinterest rather than X.
indieHackersStrategy: No IH launch documented; audience is non-technical creatives, not IH.
directOutreach: Newsletter and social pre-marketing to creative peers; Becca deliberately became the face of the company.
partnerships: Creative educators and community leaders amplify; payment/scheduling integrations secondary.
referralViral: STRONG community loop: creatives share workflows/templates; educator affiliates recruit cohorts.
aiUsage: Founder discusses leveraging AI to streamline operations (2026 podcast); product-level AI detail NOT PUBLIC.
devMethod: Husband-wife build: 10 months full build by Jake to beta deadline before baby; notebooks of ideas narrowed to focus.
soloFeasibility: LOW-MEDIUM solo: took a developer 10 months full-time; realistic for a pair (domain + builder) or patient solo with jobs.
technicalComplexity: MEDIUM-HIGH: workflow engine plus payments, scheduling and portals in one.
productComplexity: HIGH: proposals + contracts + billing + scheduling + automations in one; breadth is the moat and the burden.
infraComplexity: MEDIUM: invoicing/payments, scheduler, automations and portals must all stay reliable.
operationalComplexity: MEDIUM-HIGH: broad surface plus brand-critical reliability for wedding-season businesses; lean team by design.
supportBurden: MEDIUM-HIGH: complex all-in-one means setup questions; offset by education content and community.
salesComplexity: LOW: self-serve signup, education-heavy marketing; no sales team documented.
differentiation: Self-funded creative-first positioning: brand front-and-center (Berg rejected tools hiding her brand) plus founder accessibility.
competitiveMoat: Deep creative-workflow fit (proposals + contracts + invoices + workflows in one brandable login) plus founder-as-face trust and decade of tutorials/templates.
competitiveWeaknesses: Dated UX reputation vs HoneyBook/Honeybook-polish; feature breadth slows shipping (Dubsado 3.0 multi-year); support load from complex product.

legalPrivacy: Stores contracts, client PII and payments; compliance detail NOT PUBLIC.
acquisitionDifficulty: MEDIUM: community-led decade-long compound; slow, not fast.
monetizationDifficulty: LOW: single Premier plan with annual discount; trial-to-paid converts on real client usage, not timer pressure.

The money that we make is the money that we're able to spend'; Built In LA: 'Founded in 2016... occupies rare air as a self-funded startup'; Boss Project: 'Jake spent the next 10 months building... launched the beta version to their email list'.
